name: Propolis

lead: Propolis is the resin bees blend with wax to seal their hives. A K-beauty staple in ampoules and creams, it is used to calm breakouts, soothe skin and give a glowy finish, building on a long folk-medicine history.

Lab studies attribute antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory activity to its flavonoids and phenolics, including CAPE, which inhibits NF-kappa B signalling in cell experiments. Composition varies widely by origin. Human trials on cosmetic skin outcomes were not found; registered clinical trials concern uses such as oral health.

paras: People use propolis ampoules, creams and spot treatments as part of layered K-beauty routines, often for blemish-prone, irritated or dull skin. It is also sold as a supplement.

Contact allergy is the main documented risk, with skin inflammation and lip swelling reported from topical products, especially in people sensitive to bee products. It is sold as a cosmetic ingredient and supplement; no special approval for skin benefits is reported.

angle.text: Propolis is used in K-beauty ampoules and creams to calm breakouts, soothe skin and give a glowy finish. Lab studies show antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory activity; skin-specific human trials were not found.

lead: Propolis, also called bee glue, is a sticky resinous mixture that honey bees make from plant exudates such as tree-bud resins and sap, combined with beeswax and saliva. Bees use it to seal gaps in the hive and to coat its interior surfaces [1][2]. Its composition varies with the hive's location, season and local plants, and it typically includes flavonoids, phenolic acids and terpenoids [2].

In skincare, propolis appears as an extract in K-beauty and natural-cosmetic products, where brands market it for soothing, blemish-prone and dull-looking skin. Proponents point to its long traditional use and to laboratory findings of antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory activity [3][4].

Published evidence for cosmetic skin benefits in humans is limited. Most of the literature consists of laboratory and review work on propolis constituents, and clinical trials registered for propolis concern other uses such as oral health and general medicine. Propolis is also a recognised cause of allergic contact dermatitis [2].
infobox: Topical extract, tincture, ointment; oral supplements
Flavonoids, phenolic acids, terpenoids (varies by origin)

paras: Propolis is a variable natural product. Its chemistry depends on the plants bees visit, and researchers classify it into types such as poplar-type in temperate regions, birch-type, and tropical varieties like Brazilian green propolis, which is rich in artepillin C [1]. Fixed percentage breakdowns of resin, wax, oils and pollen are often quoted, but Wikipedia notes these are not well substantiated [2].

Flavonoids are a major constituent class and have been reviewed for antimicrobial and other biological activities [5][6]. Caffeic acid phenethyl ester (CAPE), a propolis component, inhibited activation of the transcription factor NF-kappa B in a 1996 laboratory study [7].

Propolis extracts are included in serums, ampoules, masks and spot treatments sold in Korean and natural-skincare lines, usually with claims about calming, hydrating or clarifying skin. No cosmetic-specific trial is listed in the reviewed literature that quantifies effects on wrinkles, pigmentation or acne.

Writers describe propolis use in traditional medicine since antiquity, including wound care and antiseptic applications in Egyptian, Greek and Roman sources, though dating claims come from secondary summaries [1]. Researchers have reviewed its antibacterial, antifungal and antiviral activity across propolis of different geographic origin [4], and its potential as a source of new drugs [6].

Clinical research on propolis as a whole is mostly outside skincare. Registered or completed trials have examined propolis for hand-foot-and-mouth disease, COVID-19, mouthwash and periodontal health, radiotherapy-induced oral mucositis, dentin hypersensitivity, insulin resistance and cardiometabolic outcomes [8][9][10]. Wikipedia reports that a 2026 review found possible plaque reductions with very low certainty, that mucositis studies were small with blinding problems, and that a meta-analysis of 20 trials found lower fasting glucose and triglycerides without changes in blood pressure [2].
No controlled human study of topical propolis for wrinkles, skin tone or acne was identified among the sources reviewed for this article.

Propolis can cause allergic contact dermatitis, with reported reactions to topical products including skin inflammation, lip swelling and cheilitis [2]. A 1998 review of its biological properties and toxicity addressed both [3].

Laboratory research continues on propolis flavonoids and phenolics, including anti-inflammatory signalling and antimicrobial activity [7][5][11]. Reviews describe the variability between propolis samples as a challenge for standardisation and for comparing studies [6][11].
